## Why This Matters

Almost everything you have analysed so far arrived as a **table**: one row per observation, one column
per feature. But some of the most interesting data is not about the *things* — it is about the
**connections between them**. Who follows whom on a social platform. Which papers cite which. Which
proteins interact. Which airports have direct flights. Flatten any of these into a table and you throw
away the very thing you wanted to study: the **structure of the relationships**.

The right object is a **graph** (also called a **network**): a set of **nodes** (the things) joined by
**edges** (the connections). Once your data is a graph, a whole toolbox opens up — you can ask who is
*central*, which nodes are *bridges*, how *tight-knit* a neighbourhood is, and (next lesson) which nodes
form *communities*. And the engine underneath is one you already built: in **L18** you learned that a
table is a matrix; a graph, it turns out, is **also** a matrix — its **adjacency matrix** — and the same
dot products and matrix products you drilled there now answer questions about who-knows-whom.

The running example is the most famous small network in data science.

> **Zachary's Karate Club.** In the early 1970s the sociologist Wayne Zachary recorded the friendships
> among 34 members of a university karate club. Then the club's instructor ("Mr. Hi") and its president
> ("the Officer") fell out, and the club **split in two** — each member following one leader or the
> other. Zachary's question: could the *friendship structure alone* have predicted the split? The graph
> ships inside NetworkX (`nx.karate_club_graph()`), so we never download anything. This lesson measures
> the graph; **L26** lets an algorithm find the two factions and checks how close it gets.

## What Is a Graph?

A graph is a pair of sets: the **nodes** (or *vertices*) and the **edges** (or *links*) joining pairs of
them. That is the whole definition — everything else is vocabulary for talking about structure.

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Node** (vertex) | A thing: a person, a paper, an airport. |
| **Edge** (link) | A connection between two nodes. |
| **Neighbours** of a node | The nodes it shares an edge with. |
| **Degree** of a node | How many edges it has — its number of neighbours. |
| **Path** | A sequence of edges from one node to another. |
| **Shortest path** | The fewest-edge route between two nodes. |
| **Connected component** | A group of nodes you can reach from each other by some path. |
| **Density** | The fraction of all *possible* edges that actually exist. |

Two choices fix the *kind* of graph:

- **Directed vs. undirected.** In an **undirected** graph an edge `{u, v}` is mutual — friendship on
  Facebook, a shared flight route. In a **directed** graph edges point one way — "follows" on X, a
  citation, a one-way street. Karate-club friendship is undirected.
- **Weighted vs. unweighted.** An **unweighted** edge just says *connected or not*. A **weighted** edge
  carries a number — strength, distance, number of interactions. The built-in karate club actually
  stores interaction-count weights on its edges; when we only care about *who is tied to whom* we drop
  the weights and use the **binary** view (edge present = 1, absent = 0).

## A Graph Is a Matrix

Here is the bridge back to **L18**. Number the nodes `0, 1, ..., n-1` and build an `n x n` table `A`
where

$$A_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if nodes } i \text{ and } j \text{ are connected} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

That table is the **adjacency matrix**. For an undirected graph it is **symmetric** ($A = A^{T}$,
because if `i` is tied to `j` then `j` is tied to `i`). The same network, drawn as a picture and written
as a matrix, is the same object two ways:

![Left: Zachary's Karate Club drawn as a node-link diagram, with each node sized by its degree and the two leaders (Mr. Hi and the Officer) marked in red as the largest hubs. Right: the same network as a 34 by 34 binary adjacency matrix heatmap; filled cells mark friendships and the matrix is symmetric about the diagonal, with two visibly denser blocks foreshadowing the club's two factions. The caption notes that A[i, j] = 1 when i and j are friends and that each row sum equals that node's degree.](assets/l25_network_and_matrix.png)

And now the L18 operations *mean something*:

- **Row sum = degree.** Add up row `i` of `A` and you count node `i`'s edges. Summing every row at once
  is `A @ ones` — the **matrix-times-vector** product from L18. The adjacency matrix already knows every
  node's degree.
- **`A @ A` counts common neighbours.** The **matrix-times-matrix** product from L18, applied to `A`,
  gives a table whose `(i, j)` entry is the number of length-2 paths from `i` to `j` — that is, how many
  **friends `i` and `j` share**. On the diagonal, `(A @ A)[i, i]` is just node `i`'s degree again.

This is exactly what L18 meant by "Unit VII: the adjacency matrix." The graph is not a new kind of math
— it is linear algebra wearing a different hat.

## Who Is Important? Centrality

A natural question about any network is *which nodes matter most*. There is no single answer, because
"important" can mean different things — so there are several **centrality** measures, each capturing a
different intuition:

- **Degree centrality** — *how many* connections a node has (its degree, scaled to `[0, 1]`). The
  "social butterfly": lots of direct ties.
- **Betweenness centrality** — how often a node sits **on the shortest path** between other pairs. The
  **broker** or **bridge**: remove it and parts of the network drift apart. A node can have modest
  degree but high betweenness if it is the only link between two groups.
- **Closeness centrality** — how **near** a node is to everyone else, on average (short distances to all
  others). The well-positioned node that can reach the whole network quickly.

The instructive part is that **these can disagree**. In the karate club the Officer has the *most ties*
(top degree), but Mr. Hi is the best *bridge* (top betweenness) and the most central by distance (top
closeness). If you only ranked by degree you would miss that Mr. Hi is the structural linchpin. Choosing
the right centrality is a modelling decision, not a default. (Two more — **PageRank** and **eigenvector
centrality**, which weight a node by the importance of *its* neighbours — are where this goes next;
named here, not pursued.)

## Local Structure: Ego Networks and Clustering

Zoom in on a single node `v` and its immediate surroundings and you get its **ego network**: `v` (the
"ego"), its neighbours (the "alters"), and the edges among them. Ego networks are how you study one
person's local world without the whole graph.

Two local readings:

- **Clustering coefficient** of a node — of all the *pairs* of its neighbours, what fraction are
  themselves connected? High clustering means "my friends are friends with each other" — a tight-knit
  clique. Social networks are famously high-clustering.
- **Distances and components.** Is the graph one connected piece, or several? How many edges separate
  the two most distant nodes (the **diameter**)? Real social graphs are **small worlds**: even hundreds
  of nodes are typically just a few hops apart.

## NetworkX in One Page

NetworkX is the standard Python library for graphs. The verbs you need this lesson:

| Task | NetworkX |
|------|----------|
| Build / load a graph | `nx.Graph()`, `add_edge`, `nx.read_edgelist`, `nx.karate_club_graph()` |
| Inspect | `G.number_of_nodes()`, `G.number_of_edges()`, `G.degree()`, `G.neighbors(v)` |
| Adjacency matrix | `nx.to_numpy_array(G, weight=None)` |
| Centrality | `nx.degree_centrality`, `nx.betweenness_centrality`, `nx.closeness_centrality` |
| Local structure | `nx.ego_graph`, `nx.clustering`, `nx.connected_components` |
| Distances | `nx.shortest_path_length`, `nx.diameter` |
| Draw | `nx.draw`, `nx.spring_layout` |

For graphs with millions of nodes you would move to a faster engine (igraph, graph-tool) or an
interactive tool (Gephi); the **SNAP** repository's Facebook ego-networks are a good next dataset. For
learning the ideas, a 34-node graph you can draw entirely is exactly right.

> **Forward to L26.** We measured *one* node at a time — degree, centrality, the neighbourhood. The next
> lesson asks a **global** question: do the nodes fall into **communities** — dense groups with sparse
> links between them — and can an algorithm recover the karate club's two real factions from structure
> alone? That is **community detection**.

## FAQ

**Should friendship be a directed or undirected graph?**
Undirected — friendship (and a shared flight route, or a co-authorship) is mutual. Use a **directed**
graph when the relationship has a direction: "follows", "cites", "links to", "pays".

**Is the adjacency matrix always 0s and 1s?**
Only for an unweighted graph. For a **weighted** graph the entries are the edge weights. We use the
binary (0/1) form here because we care about the *structure* of ties; `nx.to_numpy_array(G, weight=None)`
forces it even when the graph stores weights.

**Which centrality should I use?**
It depends on the question. "Who has the most direct reach?" — degree. "Who is the critical bridge
whose removal fragments the network?" — betweenness. "Who can reach everyone fastest?" — closeness.
Report more than one; their disagreements are informative.

**Do I need the adjacency matrix if NetworkX computes degree for me?**
Not for degree itself — but the matrix view is how many graph algorithms are actually defined and
implemented (PageRank, spectral methods), and it is the cleanest way to see *why* `A @ A` counts shared
friends. It is the same data NetworkX stores, made explicit.

## Cheat-sheet

| You want... | Do this |
|-------------|---------|
| A graph from an edge list | `G = nx.Graph(); G.add_edges_from(edges)` |
| The built-in example | `G = nx.karate_club_graph()` |
| Number of nodes / edges | `G.number_of_nodes()`, `G.number_of_edges()` |
| One node's neighbours / degree | `list(G.neighbors(v))`, `G.degree(v)` |
| Binary adjacency matrix | `A = nx.to_numpy_array(G, weight=None)` |
| Degree from the matrix | `A.sum(axis=1)` |
| Shared-neighbour counts | `A @ A` (off-diagonal entries) |
| The important nodes | `nx.betweenness_centrality(G)` (and friends) |
| One node's local world | `nx.ego_graph(G, v, radius=1)` |
